# Why Buick Park Avenue Blowing Hot Air on Drivers Side?

A fresh battery installation on a Buick Park Avenue followed by an air conditioning system that delivers cold air to the passenger side but warm air to the driver's side points directly to a refrigerant distribution issue. This is not a symptom of the new battery, nor is it a simple "recharge needed" scenario where topping off the system will fix the imbalance. The core problem lies in how the liquid and gas phases of the Freon are moving through the evaporator box behind the dash.

When you replace a battery, you might assume all electrical connections reset, but mechanical systems like the HVAC blend doors and refrigerant flow remain unchanged. If the car was low on refrigerant before the battery swap, or if the system had a minor leak that went unnoticed during the install, the new charge will distribute unevenly. The evaporator acts as a heat exchanger; it needs a specific ratio of liquid refrigerant to absorb heat effectively across its entire surface area. If the distribution tubes inside the evaporator are clogged or if there is a restriction in the flow, one side will receive adequate cooling while the other receives only warm air.

The most common culprit for this specific left-right temperature disparity is a blockage in the metering device or a partially collapsed expansion tube within the evaporator core. In many GM vehicles of this era, the internal tubing that feeds liquid Freon to the evaporator can kink or become obstructed by debris left during a previous service. When this happens, the refrigerant flows freely to one side (often the passenger side) but struggles to reach the driver's side. The result is an uneven temperature map across the cabin.

Another potential cause involves the blend door actuator. Even though the air is physically being cooled on the passenger side, the system might be failing to mix the cold air with the hot cabin air correctly for the driver's output. If the blend door motor is stuck or the linkage is bent, it could direct fully cooled air only to the passenger vents while sending a mixture of hot and cold airâor just hot air from the heater coreâto the driver's side.

To diagnose this without disassembling the entire dashboard, start by checking the refrigerant pressure with a gauge set while the A/C is running on high fan speed. If the low-side pressure is significantly lower than the manufacturer specification for that ambient temperature, you have a restriction downstream of the compressor. You can also perform a thermal scan of the evaporator box if you remove the glove box panel to access it; feeling for a distinct temperature difference between the left and right sections of the core will confirm a flow imbalance.

If the system was recently recharged, the technician may have added gas without addressing the underlying restriction. Adding refrigerant to a blocked system only masks the problem temporarily until the remaining fluid boils off or the compressor overheats due to lack of proper suction pressure. The correct fix often involves replacing the evaporator assembly itself or cleaning out a collapsed expansion tube if accessible.
